facts.fact_text: The present case concerns the applicant's prosecution in relation to his participation in peaceful assemblies.
On 4 December 2011 the applicant took part in a rally in St Petersburg.
The rally on 4 December 2011 in St Petersburg was a protest against the alleged fraud committed during the election to the State Duma on the same day.
On 6 December 2011 the applicant took part in another protest rally relating to the recent election to the State Duma.
The protest rally on 6 December 2011 was held at around 7.30 p.m. on a weekday near one of the entrances to a metro station.
On 26 November 2012 the applicant and several other people staged a 'performance' aimed at 'reviving' the Russian Constitution.
The 'performance' on 26 November 2012 consisted of a coffin filled with brochures containing the text of the Russian Constitution, and a speech.
During the 'performance' on 26 November 2012 the applicant held a poster saying 'Let us resurrect the Constitution'.
During the 'performance' on 26 November 2012 the applicant uttered several slogans including 'Follow your own laws', 'Stop the police state' and 'We need a different Russia'.
On 31 December 2012 the applicant took part in a rally at which the police were present.
On 5 April 2013 the applicant took part in a public assembly together with fewer than twenty people near the building of the St Petersburg Administration of the Bank of Russia.

It appears that the public assembly on 5 April 2013 was aimed at carrying the message that the Russian Government needed to prevent the removal of State-owned enterprises' revenues to offshore jurisdictions.
On 27 June 2013 the applicant and five others came in front of the building of the local office of the Federal Migration Service in St Petersburg.
On 27 June 2013 one of the group put a ladder to the wall of the Federal Migration Service building in St Petersburg.
On 27 June 2013 the applicant and another person climbed by a ladder onto the balcony at the first floor of the Federal Migration Service building in St Petersburg.
On the balcony of the Federal Migration Service building on 27 June 2013 the applicant and another person shouted the slogans 'FMS in Dushanbe' and 'Freedom to the people'.
On the balcony of the Federal Migration Service building on 27 June 2013 the applicant and another person unfolded a red flag with a white circle with a picture of a grenade.
The applicant was arrested following the rally on 4 December 2011 and taken to the police station.

On 7 February 2012 a justice of the peace sentenced the applicant to a fine of 700 Russian roubles (approximately 18 euros) for an offence under Article 19.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences.

On 7 February 2012 a justice of the peace sentenced the applicant to a fine of 700 Russian roubles (approximately 18 euros) for an offence under Article 20.2 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
On 26 March 2012 the Kirovo-Chepetskiy District Court of the Kirov Region upheld the trial judgments relating to the 4 December 2011 rally.
On 22 June 2012 the Deputy President of the Kirov Regional Court confirmed the applicant's conviction under Article 19.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences on review.
On 6 September 2012 the Deputy President of the Kirov Regional Court confirmed the applicant's conviction under Article 20.2 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences on review.
The police arrested a number of people, including the applicant, at the rally on 6 December 2011.

On 7 December 2011 a justice of the peace sentenced the applicant to eleven days of detention for the offence under Article 19.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences arising from the rally on 6 December 2011.
On 12 March 2012 the Kuybyshevskiy District Court of St Petersburg heard the applicant and upheld the judgment of 7 December 2011 in substance.
On 10 April 2012 the St Petersburg City Court upheld the court decisions relating to the rally on 6 December 2011.
On 17 August 2012 the Supreme Court of Russia upheld the court decisions relating to the rally on 6 December 2011 on the second review.
After the 'performance' on 26 November 2012 ended, the applicant was arrested and taken to the local police station.

On 17 December 2012 a justice of the peace sentenced the applicant to a fine of 15,000 Russian roubles (approximately 373 euros) under Article 20.2 § 5 of the Code of Administrative Offences in relation to the 'performance' on 26 November 2012.
On 6 June 2014 the Kuybyshevskiy District Court of St Petersburg upheld the judgment relating to the 'performance' on 26 November 2012 in a summary manner.
On 9 September 2014 the St Petersburg City Court upheld the court decisions relating to the 'performance' on 26 November 2012.
The applicant was arrested during the rally on 31 December 2012, allegedly prior to hearing any specific order from the police and, a fortiori, prior to disobeying any such order.

By a judgment issued on 1 January 2013 the Kuybyshevskiy District Court of St Petersburg sentenced the applicant to a fine of 700 Russian roubles (approximately 17 euros) under Article 19.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences in relation to the rally on 31 December 2012.

By a separate judgment issued on 1 January 2013 the Kuybyshevskiy District Court of St Petersburg sentenced the applicant to a fine of 20,000 Russian roubles (approximately 497 euros) under Article 20.2 § 5 of the Code of Administrative Offences in relation to the rally on 31 December 2012.

At the closure of the appeal hearing on 31 January 2013 the St Petersburg City Court delivered the operative part of the appeal decisions upholding the trial judgments relating to the rally on 31 December 2012.
On 12 April 2013 the Deputy President of the St Petersburg City Court confirmed the court decisions relating to the rally on 31 December 2012 on review.
According to the applicant, when the public assembly on 5 April 2013 was about to end, the police arrived and arrested him and some other participants.

With reference to a video recording, the applicant was sentenced to a fine of 1,000 Russian roubles (approximately 21 euros) under Article 19.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences for disobedience to a lawful police order to disperse, despite a repeated order from the police, in relation to the assembly on 5 April 2013.

On 10 June 2013 the Nevskiy District Court of St Petersburg convicted the applicant under Article 20.2 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences for organising and holding the public event on 5 April 2013 that had not been notified to the competent authority.
On 20 August 2013 the St Petersburg City Court upheld the judgment of 10 June 2013 relating to the assembly on 5 April 2013.
On 21 November 2013 the Deputy President of the St Petersburg City Court reclassified the case relating to the assembly on 5 April 2013 under Article 20.2 § 5 of the Code of Administrative Offences.

The Deputy President of the St Petersburg City Court sentenced the applicant on 21 November 2013 to a fine of 20,000 Russian roubles (approximately 450 euros at the time) in relation to the assembly on 5 April 2013.
On 11 March 2014 the Supreme Court of Russia upheld the judgment of 21 November 2013 relating to the assembly on 5 April 2013.
Police officers arrived at the Federal Migration Service building and took the applicant to the local police station following the 'performance' on 27 June 2013.

On 8 October 2013 the Dzerzhinskiy District Court of St Petersburg convicted the applicant under Article 20.2 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences and sentenced him to a fine of 20,000 Russian roubles (approximately 456 euros) in relation to the 'performance' on 27 June 2013.

On 19 December 2013 the St Petersburg City Court reclassified the charge relating to the 'performance' on 27 June 2013 under Article 20.2 § 5 of the Code of Administrative Offences and upheld the fine of 20,000 Russian roubles.

The police officer shown in the video indicated that the rally was therefore in breach of the Federal Law on Gatherings, Meetings, Demonstrations, Processions and Pickets, no. 54-FZ of 19 June 2004 (the Public Events Act).

On both charges arising from the 4 December 2011 rally, the justice of the peace held that the public event in the form of a meeting (митинг) had not been notified to the competent authority in breach of section 5 of the Public Events Act.

On both charges arising from the 4 December 2011 rally, the justice of the peace held that the public event in the form of a meeting (митинг) had not been notified to the competent authority in breach of sub-paragraph 2 of paragraph 3 of section 6 of the Public Events Act.

The police compiled an offence report in respect of the applicant following the rally on 6 December 2011, indicating that the rally in the form of a meeting was in breach of section 6 § 3 (2) of the Public Events Act.
The provisions of domestic law directly relevant to the present case are set out in the relevant legal framework section of the judgment.

The Federal Law on Gatherings, Meetings, Demonstrations, Processions and Pickets, no. 54-FZ of 19 June 2004 (the Public Events Act) provides that the organiser of a public event must notify the executive or municipal authority of the event pursuant to sections 5 and 7 of the Act.

Section 6 § 3 of the Public Events Act provides that during a public event participants must comply with all lawful instructions given by the event organiser, the persons designated by the organiser, the designated representative of the executive authority of the constituency of the Russian Federation or the municipality, or by law enforcement officers.
Section 6 § 3 of the Public Events Act provides that during a public event participants must respect the public order (общественный порядок) and the programme of the public event.

Section 6 § 3 of the Public Events Act provides that during a public event participants must comply with regulations aimed at ensuring transport safety and traffic security where vehicles are used for the public event.

In June 2012 section 6 § 4 was added to the Public Events Act, providing that public event participants are not allowed to cover their face, including by way of using masks or other objects specially designed to impede a person's identification.

Section 6 § 4 of the Public Events Act, added in June 2012, provides that public event participants are not allowed to be in possession of arms or objects used as such, beer or beverages produced from it.
Section 6 § 4 of the Public Events Act, added in June 2012, provides that public event participants are not allowed to be in a state of alcoholic intoxication at the venue of the public event.

Article 19.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences provided at the relevant time that disobedience to a lawful order or request made by a police officer, a military officer or a detention facility officer in connection with the exercise of duties relating to securing public order and public safety was punishable with a fine of 500 to 1,000 Russian roubles or administrative detention for up to fifteen days.

Article 19.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences provided at the relevant time that resistance to a police officer, military officer or detention facility officer in the exercise of their official duties was punishable with a fine of 500 to 1,000 Russian roubles or administrative detention for up to fifteen days.

Article 20.2 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences provided, prior to June 2012, that violation of the rules for running a public event was punishable by a fine of 1,000 to 2,000 Russian roubles as regards organisers.

Article 20.2 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences provided, prior to June 2012, that violation of the rules for running a public event was punishable by a fine of 500 to 1,000 Russian roubles for participants.

Since June 2012 Article 20.2 of the Code of Administrative Offences was amended to contain a new paragraph 5 concerning participants, providing that violation by a participant in a public event of the rules for running a public event was punishable with a fine of from 10,000 to 20,000 Russian roubles or up to forty hours of community work.

The Kuybyshevskiy District Court of St Petersburg stated that the meeting on 6 December 2011 had been held next to an entrance to a metro station during the time when the passenger traffic had been intense.

The Kuybyshevskiy District Court of St Petersburg stated that in view of the political nature of the event on 6 December 2011 entailing expressions of discontent and the large number of demonstrators, there had been a 'real threat to other people'.

The video relating to the rally on 4 December 2011 showed a police officer speaking through a loudspeaker and indicating that the rally had not received official approval from the competent authority.
The police officer shown in the video indicated that participants' actions could amount to an administrative offence.
The text of the police officer's announcement was repeated, in nearly identical terms, several times in the video relating to the rally on 4 December 2011.

On both charges arising from the 4 December 2011 rally, the justice of the peace held that the police had informed the participants of the breach several times and had instructed them to stop the meeting and to disperse.

In his appeal before the Kirovo-Chepetskiy District Court of the Kirov Region, the applicant argued that there had been no evidence that he personally (rather than the event itself or other people) had not complied with the statutory obligation to respect the 'public order' under sub-paragraph 2 of paragraph 3 of section 6 of the Public Events Act.

The offence report compiled following the rally on 6 December 2011 indicated that Officer A. and other officers had made several warnings to the participants, specifying the breach of section 6 § 3 (2) of the Public Events Act and instructing them to disperse.

The offence report compiled following the rally on 6 December 2011 indicated that the applicant had not complied with the order to disperse and thereby committed an offence under Article 19.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences.

The Kuybyshevskiy District Court of St Petersburg stated that the meeting on 6 December 2011 had been held next to an entrance to a metro station during the time when the passenger traffic had been intense.

The Kuybyshevskiy District Court of St Petersburg stated that in view of the political nature of the event on 6 December 2011 entailing expressions of discontent and the large number of demonstrators, there had been a 'real threat to other people'.
The justice of the peace considered that the 'performance' on 26 November 2012 amounted to a 'public event' regulated under the Public Events Act.
The justice of the peace considered that the 'performance' on 26 November 2012 had not been notified to the competent authority and 'had been in breach of section 6 of the Public Events Act'.

The applicant appealed his conviction arising from the 'performance' on 26 November 2012, arguing that a lawful conviction under paragraph 5 of Article 20.2 of the Code of Administrative Offences required proof that as a participant he had breached the obligations or bans listed in section 6 §§ 3 and 4 of the Public Events Act.

The applicant argued in his appeal that neither the offence report nor the trial judgment described or held against him any failure to comply with any ban or obligation under section 6 §§ 3 and 4 of the Public Events Act.

The St Petersburg City Court held on 9 September 2014 that by holding a poster and distributing leaflets the applicant had taken part in a 'public event' which had not been notified to the competent authority.

The Kuybyshevskiy District Court of St Petersburg held in relation to the charge under Article 20.2 § 5 of the Code of Administrative Offences arising from the rally on 31 December 2012 that a police officer had informed the participants that the event had not been notified and 'had explained the consequences of taking part in such an event'.

The St Petersburg City Court held in relation to the charge under Article 20.2 § 5 of the Code of Administrative Offences arising from the rally on 31 December 2012 that the participants 'had been publicly notified by a police officer about the violation of the law'.

On appeal in relation to the assembly on 5 April 2013, the St Petersburg City Court watched the video recording and concluded that a police officer had once pronounced a phrase that the event had been unlawful.

The St Petersburg City Court concluded on appeal that the video recording relating to the assembly on 5 April 2013 did not confirm that the police officer had made any repeated statements or orders to cease participation in the event.
The St Petersburg City Court noted on appeal that the police officer had not been examined at the trial as regards the relevant circumstances of the assembly on 5 April 2013.

The St Petersburg City Court held on 20 August 2013 that it was irrelevant for the offence under paragraph 2 of Article 20.2 of the Code of Administrative Offences whether the police had ordered a dispersal.

In his application for review of the court decisions relating to the assembly on 5 April 2013, the applicant argued, referring to the video recording, that the police had only announced once their position on the legality of the event while making no specific order to disperse, and even less repeating any such order.

The Deputy President of the St Petersburg City Court held on 21 November 2013 that a participant's obligations as provided by law are not related to the fact whether that person took part in a public event which was or was not approved by the executive authority.

The Deputy President of the St Petersburg City Court held on 21 November 2013 that irrespective of whether a public event was approved, a participant is required to comply with the obligations and bans provided for by the Public Events Act.

The Deputy President of the St Petersburg City Court held on 21 November 2013 that the applicant had participated in a public event in the form of a meeting on 5 April 2013 which had not been approved by the competent authority, and was therefore a participant rather than the organiser of that event.

The Deputy President of the St Petersburg City Court held on 21 November 2013 that by participating in the meeting on 5 April 2013 and after being informed by the police that it was being held in breach of the notification requirement under the Public Events Act, the applicant did not comply with the lawful order from the police to stop the meeting and to disperse.

The Deputy President of the St Petersburg City Court held on 21 November 2013 that the applicant had violated the obligations imposed on him as a participant of a public event, namely the obligation to comply with all lawful instructions from the police, and that his actions should be classified under paragraph 5 of Article 20.2 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
The Deputy President of the St Petersburg City Court noted on 21 November 2013 that the applicant had previously been prosecuted for similar offences.

The Supreme Court of Russia confirmed on 11 March 2014, inter alia, that a participant's statutory obligations under section 6 § 3 of the Public Events Act applied both to notified and non-notified public events.

The police considered that the 'performance' on 27 June 2013 amounted to an assembly regulated by the Public Events Act and thus required a prior notification to the St Petersburg city administration, but no such notification had been submitted.

The Dzerzhinskiy District Court of St Petersburg considered that the 'performance' on 27 June 2013 concerned criticism of the legislation on migration and amounted to a 'public event' regulated by the Public Events Act, specifically a group static demonstration (a 'picketing').

The Dzerzhinskiy District Court of St Petersburg considered that the applicant was the organiser of the 'performance' on 27 June 2013 and that he had not notified it to the competent authority in breach of the Public Events Act.
On 19 December 2013 the St Petersburg City Court considered that the applicant had participated in the demonstration on 27 June 2013 and had not been its organiser.

The St Petersburg City Court held on 19 December 2013 that Article 20.2 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences only concerns an organiser of a public event who violated section 5 § 5 of the Public Events Act prohibiting running a public event without notifying a public authority.

The St Petersburg City Court held on 19 December 2013 that a participant's action or inaction during a public event should be classified under paragraph 5 of Article 20.2 of the Code of Administrative Offences.

The St Petersburg City Court held on 19 December 2013 that since the applicant had participated in the static demonstration on 27 June 2013 which had not been notified to the competent authority, he had acted as a participant rather than the organiser of that demonstration.

The St Petersburg City Court noted on 19 December 2013 that the applicant had already been convicted of similar offences in 2012 and 2013 and decided that the fine of 20,000 Russian roubles was appropriate.

Pursuant to section 16 of the Public Events Act, the grounds for ending a public event shall be the emergence of a genuine threat to citizens' lives or health, and to the possessions of physical or legal persons.

Pursuant to section 16 of the Public Events Act, the grounds for ending a public event shall include commission by the participants of unlawful acts or a deliberate breach by the organiser of the rules for the conduct of public events established by the Act.
Pursuant to section 16 of the Public Events Act, since 2012 the grounds for ending a public event include non-compliance by the organisers with the obligations set out in section 5 of the Act.

Section 17 of the Public Events Act provides that if it is decided to end the public event, the representative of the executive or municipal authority shall give an order to the organiser of the public event to end the public event, having explained the reasons for its termination, and within twenty-four hours shall issue this order in writing and serve it on the organiser.
Section 17 of the Public Events Act provides that the representative of the executive or municipal authority shall set the time for compliance with the order to end the public event.

Section 17 of the Public Events Act provides that if the organiser does not comply with the order to end the public event, the representative of the executive or municipal authority shall directly address the participants of the public event and set an additional time for compliance with the order to end the public event.
Section 17 of the Public Events Act provides that in the event of non-compliance with the order to end the public event, the police shall take the necessary measures to end the public event.

Section 17 of the Public Events Act provides that the procedure for ending a public event shall not apply in the event of mass disorder, mob violence, arson, or other situations requiring urgent action.

On 26 June 2018 the Plenary of the Supreme Court of the Russian Federation adopted the Resolution 'On certain questions arising during judicial examination of administrative cases and cases on administrative offences related to the application of the legislation on public events'.

The Supreme Court of the Russian Federation's Resolution of 26 June 2018 provided guidelines indicating that the violation by a participant in a public event of the established procedure for running a public event — constituting an offence under Article 20.2 § 5 of the Code of Administrative Offences — is only established where the demonstrator did not comply with one of the obligations and prohibitions incumbent on demonstrators under section 6 §§ 3 and 4 of the Public Events Act, including the obligation to comply with all legal orders made by the police, military officers or National Guard officers.

The Supreme Court of the Russian Federation's Resolution of 26 June 2018 provided guidelines indicating that the failure by a participant in a public event to comply with lawful orders or instructions of the police was to be classified under Article 20.2 § 5 of the Code of Administrative Offences, which was in these circumstances to be regarded as a lex specialis in relation to Article 19.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences (§ 33 of the Resolution).

In Ruling no. 19-P of 17 May 2021 the Constitutional Court of the Russian Federation held that the constitutional right of peaceful assembly implies a real opportunity — through organising and participating in public events regulated under the Public Events Act — to influence the activities of public authorities by way of maintaining a civilised dialogue between civic society and the State.

The Constitutional Court of the Russian Federation held in Ruling no. 19-P of 17 May 2021 that the constitutional right of peaceful assembly does not exclude the protest nature of public events or criticism directed at specific acts or actions on the part of public authorities or at their policies.

The Constitutional Court of the Russian Federation held in Ruling no. 19-P of 17 May 2021 that the authorities' reaction to public events should be neutral and — irrespective of political, cultural or other views expressed by organisers or demonstrators — should be aimed at facilitating the lawful exercise of freedom of peaceful assembly.

The Constitutional Court of the Russian Federation held in Ruling no. 19-P of 17 May 2021 that legislative, regulatory or other measures on the part of public authorities should not unjustifiably restrict the constitutional right of peaceful assembly, and that restrictions should be based on the principles of necessity and proportionality, with due regard to the presumption in favour of the organisers' and demonstrators' willingness to maintain the peaceful nature of the event.

The Constitutional Court of the Russian Federation held in Ruling no. 19-P of 17 May 2021 that Article 20.2 of the Code of Administrative Offences, which uses a 'blanket reference' technique, should be interpreted and applied with reference to the contents of the relevant legislation and regulations, and that it is precisely their breach — specifically as regards the notification procedure for public events — that constitutes an element of the administrative offence.

Section 13 § 1 (1) and (7) of the Police Act (Federal Law no. 3-FZ of 7 February 2011) provides that outside the context of public events being held lawfully, the police is authorised to make an oral order requiring citizens to disperse or to go to another location where the amassing of people poses a threat to their lives or health, the lives or health of other citizens, possessions, or interferes with the work of organisations or impedes the traffic of vehicles or pedestrians.
